items.answer: Dijkstra finalises a node when it is the closest unvisited node, assuming that any other route to it must be at least as long. A negative edge can later shorten a path to an already finalised node. Example (directed): S->A weight 2, S->B weight 3, B->A weight -2. Dijkstra finalises A with distance 2 first, but the shortest path S->B->A has length 1.
items.method: Explain the greedy invariant (distance of a finalised node cannot improve) and show a counterexample.

items.answer: Theta(n^2): the inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, n * n calls
items.method: Multiply the iteration counts of nested independent loops.

items.answer: Theta(n^2): the number of calls is 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2
items.method: Arithmetic series for the triangular loop nest.

items.answer: Theta(n log n): the while loop doubles i, so it runs ceil(log2 n) times, and each time the inner loop makes n calls
items.method: A doubling counter gives a logarithmic number of outer iterations, multiplied by the inner cost n.

items.answer: Theta(n): the inner loop makes n + n/2 + n/4 + ... + 1 calls, a geometric series that sums to less than 2n
items.method: Geometric series: the total is dominated by the first term, so it is linear.

items.answer: O(2^n) (more precisely Theta(phi^n) with phi = 1.618). The function recomputes the same subproblems again and again; memoisation or an iterative loop would reduce this to O(n).
items.method: Each call makes two recursive calls, so the call tree roughly doubles with each level; overlapping subproblems are the cause.
